#### 1. mitochondrial disease  —  Tier 2 — Strong / Probable  (fitness 0.708)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-9865881, Reactome:R-HSA-611105)

**Proposed mechanism:** Pathogenic variant in TAFAZZIN (Disease A) (HGNC:29594) —DISRUPTS→ TAFAZZIN (HGNC:29594); TAFAZZIN (HGNC:29594) —DISRUPTS→ Cardiolipin biosynthesis and remodeling (GO:0006633); Cardiolipin biosynthesis and remodeling (GO:0006633) —DECREASES→ Cardiolipin (CHEBI:16806); Cardiolipin (CHEBI:16806) —DISRUPTS→ Mitochondrial respiration chain function (GO:0045237); Mitochondrial respiration chain function (GO:0045237) —LEADS_TO→ Disease A specific phenotypes (HP:0001250); Pathogenic variant in TAFAZZIN (Disease B) (HGNC:29594) —DISRUPTS→ TAFAZZIN (HGNC:29594); Mitochondrial respiration chain function (GO:0045237) —LEADS_TO→ Mitochondrial disease phenotypes (HP:0003675). Loss-of-function variants in TAFAZZIN lead to impaired cardiolipin biosynthesis and remodeling, which in turn disrupts mitochondrial respiration, causing a spectrum of phenotypes characteristic of both Disease A and mitochondrial disease B.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of a pathogenic variant in TAFAZZIN in patients with Disease A that results in a gain-of-function effect, or the absence of any pathogenic variants in TAFAZZIN in a significant proportion of Disease A patients. _(variant: rs121918101 (variant in TAFAZZIN with a gnomAD allele frequency > 0.01%))_

**Why it matters:** Targeting cardiolipin metabolism or mitochondrial function could offer therapeutic avenues for both diseases.

Loss-of-function mutations in UQCRQ and UQCRB disrupt the assembly and function of mitochondrial complex III, leading to impaired ATP synthesis and subsequent phenotypes like mitochondrial respiratory chain deficiency and lactic acidosis.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in UQCRQ or UQCRB that do not lead to reduced complex III activity or ATP production in patient-derived cells would falsify this hypothesis. _(variant: rs743252860)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanism of mitochondrial complex III dysfunction provides a basis for exploring common therapeutic strategies, such as agents that can bypass or support complex III function, or enhance mitochondrial biogenesis.
